To optimize the reaction conditions of these primary amines with isocyanates, the polyaddition of 1AQA with PPDI was investigated. The effect of reaction temperature on the inherent viscosity of the polyurea was examined in NMP at temperature between 30 and 1508C (Fig. 2). The optimized temperature range was between 60 and $1 1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$, giving polyurea with the highest molecular weights.

Thermal behavior of the polymers was studied using dynamic mechanical thermal analysis (DMTA). By increasing the temperature from 30 to $3 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$, one transition was seen for the polymers at which tan d went through a maximum. This transition was related to the glass transition temperature of the polymers. Also DSC analysis confirmed data obtained from DMTA. The glass transition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } )$was taken as the midpoint of the change in the slope of the baseline. Also, no polymer showed a clear melting endotherm which resulted from the amorphous nature of the polymers. A 100-ml, two-necked, round-bottomed flask equipped with a magnetic stirrer, nitrogen gas inlet tube, and calcium chloride drying tube was charged with 26 mmol of the 1-aminoanthraquinone and 75 ml of dry NMP. The mixture was stirred at $0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$for 0.5 hr. Then 21.6 ml of propylene oxide was added, and after about 3 min, 30 mmol of $^ { 3 , 5 \cdot }$-dinitrobenzoyl chloride was added and the mixture was stirred at $0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$for 0.5 hr. The temperature was raised to room temperature and the solution was stirred for 6 hr. The product was precipitated by pouring the content of the flask into water. Then it was filtered, washed with hot water, and dried overnight under vacuum at 708C. The yield of the reaction was about 92%.
The aforementioned procedure was applied to the synthesis of the dinitro compound. However, 2-aminoanthraquinone was used instead of 1-aminoanthraquinone. The yield of the reaction was about 95%.

75 ml of hydrazine monohydrate was added dropwise over a period of 1 hr at 858C. After the complete addition, the reaction was continued at reflux temperature for another 12 hr. To the suspension, 80 ml of tetrahydrofuran (THF) was added to re-dissolve the precipitated product, and refluxing was continued for 3 hr. The mixture was filtered to remove the Pd–C and the filtrate was poured into water. The product was filtered off, washed with hot water, and dried. The yield of the reaction was about 92%.
The aforementioned procedure was applied for the synthesis of the diamine. However 2AQN was used instead of 1AQN. The yield of the reaction was about 88%.

A round-bottomed flask equipped with an $\Nu _ { 2 }$inlet tube, condenser, and thermometer was charged with 0.005 mol of diamine and 10 ml of dry NMP. Then a solution containing 0.005 mol of diisocyanate in 10 ml of dry NMP was added in one lot to the flask contents. The solution was stirred for 1 hr at room temperature and 4 hr at $7 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$and then it was precipitated in water. The polymer was filtered, washed with hot water and methanol, and dried at vacuum oven at $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$

By increasing the temperature from 30 to $3 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$, one transition was seen for the polymers at which tan d went through a maximum. This transition was related to the glass transition temperature of the polymers.

Wide-angle X-ray diffraction (WAXD) patterns were performed at room temperature on an X-ray diffractometer (Siemens model D 5000) using a Ni-filtered Cu Ka radiation (40 kV, 25 mA) at a scanning rate of 38/min.

The crystallinity of the polymers was examined by WAXD patterns obtained by the powder specimens in the region of 2u 5–708 at room temperature. The X-ray diffraction studies of the polyureas revealed that all of the polymers were amorphous.
